workedExample.intro: Here is a model explanation, one step at a time.
steps: A search makes one comparison per level, so it needs at most height + 1 comparisons.
Each comparison rules out one branch and everything in it. This is called decrease and conquer.
The AVL rule keeps the height at most roughly 1.44 log(n + 2) − 1.328.
So with 1,000,000 keys, a search needs at most 28 comparisons, compared with up to 1,000,000 in a chain.
In conclusion, search is O(log n) because the AVL rule keeps the path short, not because the search uses balance factors.

workedExample.intro: Here is a worked decision for a contacts list.
steps: Is it searched often by key? Yes, because names are looked up all day.
Must it stay in order? Yes, because it is shown alphabetically.
Can keys arrive sorted? Yes, because imports are often alphabetical.
How often is it updated? Rarely, compared with how often it is searched.
The decision is to use an AVL tree.

workedExample.intro: Here is a model justification for student numbers that are issued in increasing order and looked up often.
steps: A plain BST would receive the numbers in sorted order and become a chain, with O(n) search.
An AVL tree rebalances after every insertion, so its height stays O(log n).
Every lookup is therefore O(log n), which means at most 28 comparisons, even for 1,000,000 students.
The cost is a stored height in each node and some rotation work on each insertion, which is small next to the number of lookups.
